background.definition: Acute cholangitis is characterized by acute inflammation and infection in the bile duct.

list.listitem: Incidence of cholangitis was 3% in a series of 122 patients with gallstone pancreatitis.
Incidence of primary sclerosing cholangitis in Great Britain was 0.4/100,000/year and prevalence was 3.8/100,000 in 2001.
Incidence of primary sclerosing cholangitis in the United States was 1.2/100,000/year in men and 0.5/100,000/year in women.
Typical ranges in case series between 1952 and 1989 are choledocholithiasis (32%-70%), benign biliary stenosis (5%-28%), malignant stenosis (13%-36%), and sclerosing cholangitis (0%- 3%).
Cholangitis may occur iatrogenically and after endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
Rare causes include parasites, duodenal diverticula, and blood clot.
Mirrizzi's syndrome: mechanical pressure and/or inflammatory changes caused by the presence of stones in the gallbladder neck and cystic duct.
Lemmel syndrome: duodenal parapapillary diverticulum compresses or displaces the opening of the bile duct and obstructs the passage of bile.

The onset of acute cholangitis involves increased bacteria in the bile and elevated intraductal pressure. This allows translocation of bacteria or endotoxins into the vascular system (cholangio-vascular reflux).
In acute cholangitis, with the elevated biliary pressure, the bile ductules become more permeable to translocation of bacteria and toxins.

Clinical findings associated with acute cholangitis include abdominal pain, jaundice, and fever/chills. This is known as Charcot's triad and is present in 40% to 70% of patients with acute cholangitis. C
Order CBC with platelets, CRP, hepatic transaminases, metabolic profile, and INR to confirm diagnosis and assess severity. C
Abdominal sonogram and CT scans are recommended in patients with acute cholangitis to identify the underlying pathology and plan treatment. B

list.listitem:
The diagnostic criteria given below were proposed at the Tokyo Consensus Meeting. Suspected diagnosis of cholangitis is defined as 2 or more items in A, while definite diagnosis is either items A2, A3, and A4 or 2 or more items in A plus B1, B2, and C.
A: (1) History of biliary disease, (2) fever and/or chills, (3) jaundice, (4) abdominal pain (RUQ or upper abdominal). B: (1) Evidence of inflammatory response (eg, abnormal WBC, increased CRP) and (2) abnormal hepatic transaminases. C: Biliary dilatation, or evidence of an etiology (stricture, stone, stent, etc.).
The classic features of pain, fever and/or chills, and jaundice are called Charcot's triad. They occur in about 40% to 70% of patients with acute cholangitis.

Adding confusion and hypotension as the fourth and fifth findings is termed Reynold's pentad. These features are seen in about one-third of patients and are associated with severe cholangitis and higher morbidity and mortality.
Hypotension may be the only presenting feature in elderly patients or in patients on steroids, while septic shock in severe cases can lead to multiorgan failure.

If cholangitis is suspected, order a CBC with platelets, CRP, hepatic transaminases, bilirubin, serum creatinine, and INR to confirm diagnosis and assess severity. Blood cultures and arterial blood gas are also helpful for severity assessment as well as selection of antimicrobials. Elevated amylase and/or lipase help identify complications such as choledocholithiasis causing biliary pancreatitis.

Abdominal ultrasound is there commended initial study in patients with suspected biliary inflammation or infection. CT with IV contrast is recommended for all patients with acute cholangitis since the findings are complementary to those of ultrasound. The role of imaging study is to determine the presence of biliary obstruction, level of obstruction, and cause of obstruction, for example, stricture and/orstones.
In a recent case-control study, 2 features (papillitis and marked early in homogeneous enhancement of the liver) were key findings for distinguishing suppurative from nonsuppurative cholangitis.
Bile and blood cultures are recommended to guide antibiotic selection.
Suspect cholangitis in patients at risk (choledocholithiasis, recent ERCP or surgery, GI malignancy) presenting with fever, pain, and/or jaundice.
See Prognosis section for definition of severity.
All patients should have medical therapy (IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesia) and eventual treatment of the underlying cause.
Patients with moderate cholangitis should have early biliary drainage while those with evidence of severe cholangitis and evidence of organ dysfunction should have urgent biliary drainage.
Treatment is guided by the grade of severity of acute cholangitis. C
Initiate medical treatment as soon as diagnosis is suspected by making the patient NPO and providing IV fluids, antibiotics, analgesia, and close monitoring of vitals. C
Perform biliary drainage in all cases of moderate and severe cholangitis and in patients with mild disease who do not respond to noninvasive medical therapy. C
When patients are stable, perform definitive treatment of the underlying cause, such as cholecystectomy or resection of tumor or polyp. C

For patients with primary biliary cholangitis, cohort studies have found a strong association between use of UDCA and avoidance of liver transplant and death, with a NNT of 5 to 26 depending on their alkaline phosphatase level. B

Bacterial species commonly identified in patients with acute cholangitis (10%-44%) include Ecoli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Enterococcus faecalis, Pseudomonas, and Proteus organisms. Less commonly observed species (<5%) include Salmonellatyphi and paratyphi, and strep species. Anaerobes such as Clostridium and Bacteroides are seen in 1% to 10% of patients in different series.
Give antibiotics to all patients with acute cholangitis; the duration should be at least 2 to 3 days for patients with mild disease and at least 5 to 7 days for those with moderate or severe disease.

A systematic review of 4 small studies (n = 205) comparing short (≤3 days) to long (>5 days) courses of antibiotics suggested that shorter courses may be as effective as longer courses, but the quality of evidence was poor.
Recommended antibiotics for mild acute cholangitis include a first-or second-generation cephalosporin, ampicillin/sulbactam, or piperacillin/tazobactam.

Recommended antibiotics for moderate to severe acute cholangitis are a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin (eg, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime), ampicillin/sulbactam, or piperacillin/tazobactam as single agents. Alternatives include fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, and the addition of metronidazole to cover anaerobes.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) is widely recommended as initial therapy for patients with primary biliary cholangitis. While it improves serum markers of liver damage, a Cochrane review concluded that it does not improve any patient-oriented outcomes. On the other hand, large, well done cohort studies have found a strong association between use of UDCA and avoidance of liver transplant and death, with a NNT of 5 to 26 depending on their alkaline phosphatase level.

In a clinical trial, 100 patients with primary biliary cholangitis who had not responded to ursodeoxycholic acid were randomized to bezafibrate 400 mg once daily or placebo. The primary outcome of biochemical response was more likely in the intervention group (31% vs 0%, p < 0.001). However, there was no difference in the likelihood of portal hypertension (20% vs 18%).

A systematic review of 7 RCTs enrolling 279 patients concluded that bezafibrate monotherapy or in combination with UDCA improves liver biochemistry but has uncertain effects on mortality, liver-related complications, or quality of life.
There is little evidence to support or refute corticosteroid therapy for primary sclerosing cholangitis.
Similarly, the use of D-penicillamine and bile acids is not sufficiently supported by evidence. Bile acids, however, can improve disease-oriented outcomes such as liver biochemistry.
For patients with moderate cholangitis, perform early endoscopic orpercutaneous drainage. Once the patient is stable, remove the cause of the obstruction to provide definitive treatment.

For patients with severe cholangitis (), perform urgent biliary drainage followed by definitive surgical treatment once the patient is stable. The primary difference in management between moderate and severe cholangitis is the urgency of drainage and the need for additional organ support measures in severe disease.
When acute cholangitis is suspected, provide basic medical treatment: keep the patient NPO, begin IV fluids, provide analgesia, and prescribe antibiotics (see Drug Therapy section).
Assess severity (). For patients with severe comorbidities, acute pancreatitis, and malignancy as well as elderly patients, provide close monitoring for possible progress toward severe disease.
If medical treatment is not sufficient (in moderate or severe cholangitis), then consider biliary drainage via endoscopic, percutaneous, or surgical means.

For patients with severe acute cholangitis, consider organ support such as mechanical ventilation, treatment of disseminated intravascular coagulation, and management of renal failure. When the patient is stabilized, perform urgent endoscopic, percutaneous, or operative decompresion of bile duct.
Mortality ranges from 5% to 28% in case series since 1980. B
See for severity assessment criteria. C

In a recent series of 117 patients with acute cholangitis, independent predictors of organ failure or death were an admitting WBC of greater than 20,000 cells/mm3 and a total bilirubin greater than 10 mg/dL. B
In a recent case-control study, 2 features (papillitis and marked early in homogeneous enhancement of the liver) were key findings for distinguishing suppurative from nonsuppurative cholangitis. B

feature.caption: Assessment of Severity of Acute Cholangitis.
feature.feature_body:
Severity Criteria
Mild Disease that responds to initial medical treatment (fluids, antibiotics, NPO)
Moderate Disease that does not respond to initial medical treatment but is also not associated with evidence of organ dysfunction
Severe Disease associated with organ dysfunction: hypotension requiring treatment, disturbed consciousness, PaO2/FIO2 ratio <300, serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL, INR >1.5, or platelet count <100,000
Data from Mayumi T, Takada T, Kawarada Y, et al. Results of the Tokyo Consensus Meeting Tokyo guidelines. J Hepatobiliary Pancreat Surg 2007;14:114-121.
